content_voiceover: Here's a classic tumor marker pitfall tested on boards: the relationship between the Lewis blood group and CA19-9. CA19-9 is chemically Sialyl Lewis A, produced when a precursor substrate is acted on by two enzymes in sequence, first FUT3, the Lewis enzyme, converting it to Lewis A antigen, and then a sialyltransferase, often upregulated by adenocarcinoma cells, converting Lewis A into Sialyl Lewis A, which is CA19-9. Now, some people inherit two nonfunctional FUT3 alleles, genotype le over le, giving the Lewis-negative phenotype, Le a-minus b-minus. Without functional FUT3, no Lewis A antigen is ever made, so no CA19-9 can be generated, no matter how much cancer is present or how much sialyltransferase the tumor produces. This occurs in about 9% of Taiwanese and 6% of Caucasians. The board-relevant takeaway: a falsely low or undetectable CA19-9 in a Lewis-negative patient does not rule out pancreatic or biliary adenocarcinoma, you simply cannot use that marker to track disease in these patients.
keypoints: CA19-9 = Sialyl-Lewis A, built by FUT3 (Lewis enzyme) plus tumor sialyltransferase
Le(a-b-) genotype (le/le) means nonfunctional FUT3, so CA19-9 can never be produced
About 9% of Taiwanese and 6% of Caucasians are Lewis-negative
Pitfall: an undetectable CA19-9 does NOT exclude adenocarcinoma in Lewis-negative patients
